title: Quantitative relationships between occupant satisfaction and satisfaction aspects of indoor environmental quality and building design
research_question: Which subjectively evaluated indoor environmental parameters and building features mostly affect occupants' satisfaction in mainly US office buildings?

participants.description: 52,980 occupants (47% female, 36% male, 17% unknown; 7% <30 years, 18% 31-50 years, 10% >50 years, 65% unknown) from 351 office buildings, primarily in the US (78%). Most worked in cubicles with high partitions (39%) or low partitions (22%), or private offices (26%). 63% were within 4.6m of a window. Most buildings were air-conditioned (50%) and had no LEED rating (86%).
participants.recruitment: Building representatives contacted CBE for survey permission, or CBE researchers contacted building representatives.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Existing office buildings (351 unique buildings) and their various indoor environmental quality parameters and building features, as perceived by occupants.

mechanisms: The way in which building occupants perceive their space is much more important than the actual amount of space.

Preference for private offices may partly be associated with greater freedom to organize the office space, ability to control the indoor environment to a greater extent in a private office and freedom from having to negotiate the conditions with co-workers.
moderators: Type of office (single, shared, cubicles with high/low partitions)
Distance of workstation from a window (within 4.6m or further)
Satisfaction level with workspace (satisfied or dissatisfied)
implementation_implications: To maximize workspace satisfaction, designers should invest in aspects which increase satisfaction with amount of space and storage, noise level and visual privacy.
Office workers will be most satisfied with their workspace and building when located close to a window in a private office.
Knowledge about people's priorities may be used as guidelines when constructing and renovating buildings so that building occupants' satisfaction can be maximized.
Increasing occupants' satisfaction may promote higher productivity.

limitations: No systematic randomized approach in relation to building selection, with almost 80% of surveyed buildings situated in the US, limiting generalizability to American settings.

The study considered only the influence of satisfaction with 15 different indoor environmental parameters and building features on workspace satisfaction, potentially missing other relevant parameters (e.g., outside view).
Absence of physical measurements, making it difficult to relate subjective responses to objective measures of indoor environmental quality parameters and building features.

Area per person was a rough estimation and did not strongly correlate with satisfaction with amount of space, possibly due to calculation method (gross building area including common spaces, not specific workstation area) and reliance on facility manager estimates.

instruments_used.name: CBE Occupant Satisfaction Survey
instruments_used.construct: Occupant satisfaction with various aspects of indoor environmental quality and building design, and overall workspace satisfaction
instruments_used.description: A comprehensive self-report questionnaire developed by the Center for the Built Environment (CBE) at UC Berkeley, assessing satisfaction with 15 indoor environmental parameters and building features, as well as overall workspace satisfaction, comfort, health, and productivity.
